question: Which acquisition traffic sources are driving the highest AOV and items per order this year?
approach: Join users to orders and order_items, filtering for orders placed within the current calendar year. Exclude line items with status 'Cancelled' or 'Returned' to compute net revenue and valid item counts. Group by users.traffic_source to calculate distinct orders, net revenue, AOV, and items per order.
sql:
SELECT
  u.traffic_source,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders,
  COUNT(DISTINCT u.id) AS unique_customers,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS net_revenue,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(
    SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END),
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)
  ), 2) AS aov,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(
    COUNT(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.id ELSE NULL END),
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)
  ), 2) AS avg_items_per_order
FROM users AS u
JOIN orders AS o
  ON u.id = o.user_id
LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi
  ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR))
GROUP BY u.traffic_source
ORDER BY aov DESC
LIMIT 50;
report: For the current calendar year, Facebook is the acquisition traffic source driving both the highest average order value (AOV) at 67.02 and the highest basket size at 1.11 avg_items_per_order. Display produced the second-highest AOV at 64.81 (with 1.06 avg_items_per_order), while Organic and Email followed in items per order at 1.08 each (generating AOVs of 64.46 and 64.22, respectively), and Search recorded an AOV of 64.19 and 1.06 items per order. Per the approach definition, metrics reflect orders placed within the current calendar year, excluding line items with a status of 'Cancelled' or 'Returned' to calculate net revenue and valid item counts. As a follow-up, it is worth checking whether product category mix or specific marketing campaigns account for Facebook's lead, especially given its smaller volume of 2664 total orders compared to Search's 29816 total orders.

question: How have our AOV and average basket size trended month-over-month over the last 12 months?
approach: Group orders and order items over the trailing 12 completed months using DATE_TRUNC on orders.created_at. Exclude cancelled and returned lines to compute valid net revenue and units sold per the glossary. AOV is net revenue divided by distinct orders, and basket size is valid items divided by distinct orders.
sql:
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC(DATE(o.created_at), MONTH) AS order_month,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS net_revenue,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(
    SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END),
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)
  ), 2) AS aov,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(
    COUNT(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.id ELSE NULL END),
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)
  ), 2) AS avg_items_per_order
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi
  ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 12 MONTH))
GROUP BY order_month
ORDER BY order_month DESC
LIMIT 50;
report: Per the defined methodology, Average Order Value (AOV) is calculated as net revenue divided by distinct orders, and average basket size (`avg_items_per_order`) is calculated as valid items divided by distinct orders, excluding cancelled and returned lines. Between 2025-10-01 and 2026-09-01, AOV remained relatively stable, fluctuating between a low of 62.92 in 2026-02-01 and a high of 68.07 in 2026-03-01, while average basket size stayed tightly bound between 1.07 and 1.1. In the latest recorded month of 2026-10-01, both metrics dropped to period lows, with AOV declining to 57.64 (down from 65.38 in 2026-09-01) and basket size falling to 0.92 (down from 1.1 in 2026-09-01). As a follow-up, it is worth checking whether 2026-10-01 is an incomplete month or has an anomaly in returns and cancellations, as an average basket size below one indicates total valid items were fewer than total distinct orders.

question: How is our order volume and revenue distributed across order value tiers so far this year?
approach: Calculate order-level net revenue for orders created this year by aggregating order_items excluding cancelled and returned records. Bucket orders into spend tiers, then aggregate order counts, tier revenue, tier AOV, items per order, and share of overall sales.
sql:
WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT
    o.order_id,
    SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END) AS order_revenue,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.id ELSE NULL END) AS items_in_order
  FROM orders AS o
  JOIN order_items AS oi
    ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  WHERE o.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR))
  GROUP BY o.order_id
),
tiered_orders AS (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    order_revenue,
    items_in_order,
    CASE
      WHEN order_revenue < 50 THEN '1. Under $50'
      WHEN order_revenue < 100 THEN '2. $50 to $99.99'
      WHEN order_revenue < 200 THEN '3. $100 to $199.99'
      ELSE '4. $200 and above'
    END AS spend_tier
  FROM order_totals
)
SELECT
  spend_tier,
  COUNT(order_id) AS total_orders,
  ROUND(SUM(order_revenue), 2) AS tier_revenue,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(order_revenue), COUNT(order_id)), 2) AS tier_aov,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(items_in_order), COUNT(order_id)), 2) AS avg_items_per_order,
  ROUND(100.0 * SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(order_revenue), SUM(SUM(order_revenue)) OVER()), 2) AS pct_of_total_revenue
FROM tiered_orders
GROUP BY spend_tier
ORDER BY spend_tier;
report: Based on net revenue from orders created this year (excluding cancelled and returned order items), revenue is concentrated in the upper tiers while volume is skewed toward the lowest tier. The "$200 and above" tier generated the largest share of sales at 875590.88 (31.94% of total revenue) across 2783 orders with a tier AOV of 314.62, closely followed by the "$100 to $199.99" tier with 845012.89 (30.82%) across 5893 orders and an AOV of 143.39. In contrast, the "Under $50" tier drove the vast majority of volume with 25467 total orders, but accounted for only 415683.3 (15.16% of total revenue) with an AOV of 16.32, while "$50 to $99.99" accounted for 8406 orders, 605253.75 in revenue (22.08%), and an AOV of 72.0. Average items per order scaled across tiers, measuring 0.62 for "Under $50", 1.38 for "$50 to $99.99", 1.88 for "$100 to $199.99", and 2.52 for "$200 and above". As a follow-up, it is worth checking why the "Under $50" tier has an average of 0.62 items per order, specifically whether excluding cancelled and returned item records while retaining the order count deflated item metrics for partially returned or zero-item orders.

question: Did repeat customers have a higher basket value and item count than first-time buyers last quarter?
approach: Sequence customer orders over their full lifetime using ROW_NUMBER partitioned by user_id to identify first orders versus repeat orders. Filter orders to the previous calendar quarter, aggregate order items excluding cancelled/returned items, and compare order counts, net revenue, AOV, and basket size across first-time and repeat buyers.
sql:
WITH customer_order_history AS (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    user_id,
    created_at,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at) AS order_seq
  FROM orders
),
last_quarter_orders AS (
  SELECT
    coh.order_id,
    coh.user_id,
    CASE WHEN coh.order_seq = 1 THEN 'First-time Order' ELSE 'Repeat Order' END AS customer_order_type,
    SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END) AS order_revenue,
    COUNT(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.id ELSE NULL END) AS item_count
  FROM customer_order_history AS coh
  JOIN order_items AS oi
    ON coh.order_id = oi.order_id
  WHERE coh.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER), QUARTER))
    AND coh.created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))
  GROUP BY coh.order_id, coh.user_id, customer_order_type
)
SELECT
  customer_order_type,
  COUNT(order_id) AS total_orders,
  ROUND(SUM(order_revenue), 2) AS total_revenue,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(order_revenue), COUNT(order_id)), 2) AS aov,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(item_count), COUNT(order_id)), 2) AS avg_items_per_order
FROM last_quarter_orders
GROUP BY customer_order_type
ORDER BY customer_order_type;
report: No, repeat customers did not have a higher basket value or item count than first-time buyers last quarter. First-time orders generated a higher average order value (aov) of 65.12 compared to 64.09 for repeat orders, while both cohorts had an identical avg_items_per_order of 1.09 (with first-time orders totaling 8373 orders and 545264.04 in revenue, compared to 8188 orders and 524775.98 in revenue for repeat orders). These definitions were established by sequencing lifetime orders per customer using ROW_NUMBER partitioned by user_id to isolate first versus repeat purchases within the previous calendar quarter, excluding cancelled and returned items from the aggregation. As a follow-up, it is worth checking whether promotional discounting or differences in product category mix accounted for the slightly lower basket value among repeat buyers.

question: Which top 10 US states have the highest AOV over the last 90 days, and how does their average basket size compare?
approach: Filter orders from the last 90 days for customers located in the United States, keeping users.state paired with users.country. Calculate valid net revenue and units excluding cancelled and returned items, then compute AOV and average items per order for states with at least 50 orders to ensure statistical relevance.
sql:
SELECT
  u.state,
  u.country,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS total_revenue,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(
    SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END),
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)
  ), 2) AS aov,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(
    COUNT(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.id ELSE NULL END),
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)
  ), 2) AS avg_items_per_order
FROM users AS u
JOIN orders AS o
  ON u.id = o.user_id
LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi
  ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE u.country = 'United States'
  AND o.created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)
GROUP BY u.state, u.country
HAVING total_orders >= 50
ORDER BY aov DESC
LIMIT 10;
report: Based on net revenue and units from valid orders (excluding cancelled and returned items) over the last 90 days for US states with at least 50 orders, the top 10 states by average order value (AOV) are Maryland (75.17), Arizona (74.77), Georgia (73.23), Wisconsin (71.32), Pennsylvania (70.54), South Carolina (67.18), Washington (67.18), Illinois (66.74), Indiana (64.92), and Florida (64.28). Across these states, average basket size ranges narrowly between 1.0 and 1.34 items per order, led by Arizona with the highest average basket size of 1.34 items (130 orders, 9720.09 total revenue), whereas Indiana (92 orders) and Florida (344 orders) both average 1.0 item per order. Top-ranking Maryland achieved the highest AOV of 75.17 across 84 orders with an average basket size of only 1.11 items. A recommended follow-up is to examine product category mix and individual item pricing across these states to verify whether higher AOV in states like Maryland is driven by premium items rather than multi-item baskets.

question: Which active customers in the US are underspending relative to their state's median AOV?
approach: Identify active customers in the United States who placed at least one order in the trailing 90 days per the glossary. Calculate each customer's AOV over this period (excluding cancelled and returned items) and determine their state's median AOV using PERCENTILE_CONT partitioned by state and country. Filter for customers whose AOV falls below their state's median.
sql:
WITH customer_orders AS (
  SELECT
    u.id AS user_id,
    u.first_name,
    u.last_name,
    u.state,
    u.country,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders,
    SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END) AS total_revenue
  FROM users AS u
  JOIN orders AS o
    ON u.id = o.user_id
  LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi
    ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  WHERE u.country = 'United States'
    AND o.created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)
  GROUP BY u.id, u.first_name, u.last_name, u.state, u.country
  HAVING total_orders > 0
),
customer_benchmarks AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    first_name,
    last_name,
    state,
    country,
    total_orders,
    ROUND(total_revenue, 2) AS total_revenue,
    ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(total_revenue, total_orders), 2) AS customer_aov,
    ROUND(PERCENTILE_CONT(SAFE_DIVIDE(total_revenue, total_orders), 0.5) OVER(PARTITION BY state, country), 2) AS state_median_aov
  FROM customer_orders
)
SELECT
  user_id,
  first_name,
  last_name,
  state,
  country,
  total_orders,
  total_revenue,
  customer_aov,
  state_median_aov,
  ROUND(state_median_aov - customer_aov, 2) AS spend_gap
FROM customer_benchmarks
WHERE customer_aov < state_median_aov
ORDER BY spend_gap DESC
LIMIT 50;
report: Per the defined approach, active US customers are those who placed at least one order in the trailing 90 days, with customer average order value (AOV) calculated by excluding cancelled and returned items and benchmarked against the state median AOV computed via `PERCENTILE_CONT`. Across 50 identified underspending customers, the largest deficit is observed for Skyler Ruiz in Vermont, who has a customer AOV of 0.0 compared to a state median AOV of 104.5 (spend gap of 104.5). Other notable gaps include Casey Silva in New Hampshire with a customer AOV of 14.67 against a state median AOV of 90.99 (spend gap of 76.32), and Alaska customers Quinn Fischer (AOV 28.88, spend gap 68.12) and Morgan Silva (AOV 33.67, spend gap 63.33) against a state median AOV of 97.0. Multiple customers across Missouri, Nebraska, and Oklahoma also appear with a customer AOV of 0.0 against state median AOVs of 54.0, 51.5, and 51.13, respectively. A key follow-up worth investigating is why so many active customers have a total revenue and AOV of 0.0 despite having completed orders, which may indicate that all ordered items were subsequently returned or cancelled.

question: How do our top brands compare in terms of average order value (AOV) and distinct order volume so far this year?
approach: Join order_items to products for year-to-date orders, excluding cancelled and returned line items. Count distinct order IDs and sum sale prices per brand to compute average order value (AOV) as revenue divided by order count. Order the results by distinct order count to highlight top-volume brands alongside basket size.
sql:
SELECT
  p.brand,
  COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders,
  ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(oi.sale_price), COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)), 2) AS aov
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN products AS p
  ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
  AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR))
  AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(CURRENT_DATE())
GROUP BY p.brand
ORDER BY orders DESC
LIMIT 50
report: Evaluating year-to-date orders excluding cancelled and returned line items—where average order value (AOV) is defined as total revenue divided by distinct order count—Allegra K leads overall volume by a wide margin with 1471 orders but records a low AOV of 14.56. The next highest-volume brands are Calvin Klein with 792 orders (AOV of 64.17) and Carhartt with 629 orders (AOV of 69.9). In contrast, several brands maintain substantially higher basket sizes despite lower order counts, notably Diesel (392 orders, AOV of 139.33, and top revenue of 54616.54) and 7 For All Mankind (280 orders, AOV of 155.54). A worthwhile follow-up is to verify whether multi-brand orders are inflating individual brand order counts, as counting distinct order IDs per brand does not reflect whether an order was exclusive to that brand.

question: Rank our top brands by gross margin and margin percentage this year to date, split by department.
approach: Join order_items to products to calculate revenue and gross margin (sale price minus cost), excluding cancelled and returned items for the year-to-date period. Group by product department and brand to calculate margin dollars and gross margin percentage. Use DENSE_RANK partitioned by department to rank brands within Men and Women.
sql:
WITH brand_dept_metrics AS (
  SELECT
    p.department,
    p.brand,
    SUM(oi.sale_price) AS revenue,
    SUM(oi.sale_price - p.cost) AS gross_margin
  FROM order_items AS oi
  JOIN products AS p
    ON oi.product_id = p.id
  WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR))
    AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(CURRENT_DATE())
  GROUP BY p.department, p.brand
)
SELECT
  department,
  brand,
  ROUND(revenue, 2) AS revenue,
  ROUND(gross_margin, 2) AS gross_margin,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(gross_margin, revenue) * 100, 2) AS gross_margin_pct,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY department ORDER BY gross_margin DESC) AS margin_rank
FROM brand_dept_metrics
ORDER BY department, margin_rank ASC
LIMIT 50
report: For the Men's department year to date, Diesel ranks first in gross margin at 24411.38 (49.95% gross margin on 48868.83 revenue), followed by Carhartt at 19192.56 (53.42%), Calvin Klein at 17652.73 (53.48%), Tommy Hilfiger at 13359.79 (55.87%), and True Religion at 12563.14 (47.37%). While Diesel leads in total margin dollars, Ray-Ban (rank 20, gross margin 6564.25) and Joseph Abboud (rank 13, gross margin 8640.06) achieved the highest margin percentages among the top 20 Men's brands at 60.19% and 58.38%, respectively. Per the approach, gross margin is defined as sale price minus cost (excluding returned and cancelled items for the YTD period), with rankings assigned via dense rank partitioned by department on total margin dollars. question: Which brands had the highest quarter-over-quarter revenue growth comparing last quarter to the quarter before that?
approach: Aggregate revenue per brand over the two most recent completed calendar quarters by joining order_items and products, excluding cancelled and returned items. Pivot the results across the two quarters to compute both absolute dollar change and percentage revenue growth. Filter out brands without baseline revenue in the earlier quarter to avoid division-by-zero anomalies.
sql:
WITH quarterly_brand_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    p.brand,
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE(oi.created_at), QUARTER) AS quarter_start,
    SUM(oi.sale_price) AS revenue
  FROM order_items AS oi
  JOIN products AS p
    ON oi.product_id = p.id
  WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 2 QUARTER), QUARTER))
    AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))
  GROUP BY p.brand, quarter_start
),
pivoted AS (
  SELECT
    brand,
    SUM(CASE WHEN quarter_start = DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 2 QUARTER), QUARTER) THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) AS prior_q_revenue,
    SUM(CASE WHEN quarter_start = DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER), QUARTER) THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) AS last_q_revenue
  FROM quarterly_brand_revenue
  GROUP BY brand
)
SELECT
  brand,
  ROUND(prior_q_revenue, 2) AS prior_quarter_revenue,
  ROUND(last_q_revenue, 2) AS last_quarter_revenue,
  ROUND(last_q_revenue - prior_q_revenue, 2) AS revenue_growth_amount,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(last_q_revenue - prior_q_revenue, prior_q_revenue) * 100, 2) AS revenue_growth_pct
FROM pivoted
WHERE prior_q_revenue > 0
ORDER BY revenue_growth_pct DESC
LIMIT 50
report: Miss Sixty achieved the highest quarter-over-quarter revenue growth at 1740.44% (revenue increasing from 75.0 to 1380.33, a growth amount of 1305.33), followed by Amanda Uprichard at 1519.2% (from 25.0 to 404.8) and Gypsy 05 at 1445.71% (from 17.5 to 270.5). UniformTux and Catherine Malandrino rounded out the top five, posting growth rates of 1426.92% (from 6.5 to 99.25) and 1216.93% (from 61.37 to 808.2), respectively. In accordance with the defined approach, revenue was calculated across the two most recent completed calendar quarters by joining product and order item data, excluding cancelled and returned items, and filtering out brands without earlier-quarter baseline revenue. As a caveat and follow-up worth checking, the highest percentage increases are heavily driven by low baseline revenues in the prior quarter, so analyzing performance with a minimum revenue threshold or sorting by absolute revenue growth (such as Club Room's 1409.0 increase) would better highlight material volume changes.

question: Which brands had the highest return rate over the last 90 days, and how much revenue did they generate?
approach: Compute total line items and returned items per brand by joining order_items to products over the trailing 90 days. Return rate is calculated as returned items divided by total items, while revenue sums sale prices excluding cancelled and returned items. Filter out brands with low order volume (fewer than 50 total items) to avoid statistical outliers.
sql:
SELECT
  p.brand,
  COUNT(oi.id) AS total_items,
  COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned') AS returned_items,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned'), COUNT(oi.id)) * 100, 2) AS return_rate_pct,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS revenue
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN products AS p
  ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)
GROUP BY p.brand
HAVING total_items >= 50
ORDER BY return_rate_pct DESC
LIMIT 50
report: Among qualifying brands with at least 50 total items ordered over the last 90 days, Sutton Studio recorded the highest return rate at 21.13% (15 returned items out of 71 total items) while generating 5168.03 in revenue. The next highest return rates were observed for MANGO at 19.23% (10 returned of 52 items; 1724.66 revenue), Russell Athletic at 19.05% (12 returned of 63 items; 1209.14 revenue), NEFF at 18.18% (10 returned of 55 items; 1633.2 revenue), and PUMA at 16.98% (9 returned of 53 items; 1457.12 revenue). Per the approach, return rate is computed as returned items divided by total line items, revenue reflects the sum of sale prices excluding cancelled and returned items, and brands with fewer than 50 items were filtered out. A key follow-up worth checking is the return window lag, as orders placed toward the end of the 90-day period may not have completed their return eligibility window yet.

question: What were our top 10 brands by revenue last quarter, and what share of total catalog revenue did each represent?
approach: Join order_items to products on product_id, filtering for line items created during the previous calendar quarter. Calculate revenue as total sale price excluding cancelled and returned line items. Use an analytic window function to compute each brand's revenue share of the total quarterly revenue across all brands.
sql:
WITH brand_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    p.brand,
    ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue
  FROM order_items AS oi
  JOIN products AS p
    ON oi.product_id = p.id
  WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER), QUARTER))
    AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))
  GROUP BY p.brand
)
SELECT
  brand,
  revenue,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(revenue, SUM(revenue) OVER ()) * 100, 2) AS revenue_share_pct
FROM brand_revenue
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 10
report: During the previous calendar quarter, revenue was measured as total sale price excluding cancelled and returned line items, with revenue share computed as each brand's percentage of total catalog revenue across all brands. The top five brands by revenue were Diesel at 19716.91 (1.85% share), Calvin Klein at 19213.95 (1.81%), Carhartt at 17064.5 (1.6%), True Religion at 16132.02 (1.52%), and 7 For All Mankind at 15270.18 (1.43%). The remaining top 10 brands were Joe's Jeans at 11788.66 (1.11%), The North Face at 11589.53 (1.09%), Tommy Hilfiger at 11267.69 (1.06%), Columbia at 11107.84 (1.04%), and Volcom at 10892.78 (1.02%). As a follow-up, it is worth checking the return lag to ensure items created near the end of the quarter were not returned in the subsequent quarter, which could affect final realized revenue figures.

question: For our top 5 brands by revenue over the last 12 months, what is their revenue breakdown across our top 5 countries?
approach: Identify the top 5 brands and top 5 countries by total revenue over the trailing 365 days in separate subqueries. Join order_items, products, and users to break down recognized revenue by brand and country, excluding cancelled and returned orders. Filter to include only the intersections of the top 5 brands and top 5 countries.
sql:
WITH top_brands AS (
  SELECT
    p.brand,
    SUM(oi.sale_price) AS brand_revenue
  FROM order_items AS oi
  JOIN products AS p
    ON oi.product_id = p.id
  WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 365 DAY)
  GROUP BY p.brand
  ORDER BY brand_revenue DESC
  LIMIT 5
),
top_countries AS (
  SELECT
    u.country,
    SUM(oi.sale_price) AS country_revenue
  FROM order_items AS oi
  JOIN users AS u
    ON oi.user_id = u.id
  WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 365 DAY)
  GROUP BY u.country
  ORDER BY country_revenue DESC
  LIMIT 5
)
SELECT
  p.brand,
  u.country,
  ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN products AS p
  ON oi.product_id = p.id
JOIN users AS u

question: How many active versus churned customers do we have across our top countries right now?
approach: Evaluates all customers who have placed at least one order by checking their most recent order date against the 90-day threshold (TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)). Customers with an order in the last 90 days are identified as active, while those whose latest order occurred before that window are classified as churned. The query aggregates active and churned counts by normalized country, calculating the churn rate percentage for the top 50 countries by customer base.
sql:
WITH customer_activity AS (
  SELECT
    o.user_id,
    u.country,
    MAX(o.created_at) AS last_order_at
  FROM orders AS o
  JOIN users AS u
    ON o.user_id = u.id
  GROUP BY o.user_id, u.country
)
SELECT
  country,
  COUNTIF(last_order_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)) AS active_customers,
  COUNTIF(last_order_at < TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)) AS churned_customers,
  COUNT(*) AS total_historical_customers,
  ROUND(
    100.0 * SAFE_DIVIDE(
      COUNTIF(last_order_at < TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)),
      COUNT(*)
    ),
    2
  ) AS churn_rate_pct
FROM customer_activity
GROUP BY country
ORDER BY total_historical_customers DESC
LIMIT 50;
report: Across all customers with at least one historical order, customers are defined as active if they placed an order within the last 90 days and churned if their most recent order occurred prior to that window. Among our top three markets by customer base, China has 5,489 active and 21,657 churned customers (79.78% churn rate), the United States has 3,576 active and 14,331 churned customers (80.03% churn rate), and Brazil has 2,424 active and 9,355 churned customers (79.42% churn rate). Other major countries follow a similar pattern, including South Korea (864 active, 3,349 churned), France (771 active, 3,044 churned), the United Kingdom (719 active, 2,967 churned), and Germany (676 active, 2,786 churned). As a follow-up, it is worth checking the natural repurchase cycle by product category, as a strict 90-day threshold may misclassify infrequent but loyal buyers as churned.

question: How has our monthly new customer acquisition and their initial spend trended over the last 12 months?
approach: Identifies each customer's cohort acquisition month using their earliest order timestamp from orders and filters for cohorts acquired across the trailing 12 full calendar months. It joins the customer's initial order line items from order_items (excluding Cancelled and Returned items) to compute first-order revenue and initial average order value (AOV). The results are grouped by acquisition month and ordered chronologically to track acquisition velocity and customer quality.
sql:
WITH user_first_order AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    MIN(created_at) AS first_order_at
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY user_id
),
first_orders_in_window AS (
  SELECT
    ufo.user_id,
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE(ufo.first_order_at), MONTH) AS acquisition_month,
    o.order_id
  FROM user_first_order AS ufo
  JOIN orders AS o
    ON ufo.user_id = o.user_id
   AND ufo.first_order_at = o.created_at
  WHERE ufo.first_order_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 12 MONTH), MONTH))
    AND ufo.first_order_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH))
)
SELECT
  fo.acquisition_month,
  COUNT(DISTINCT fo.user_id) AS new_customers,
  COUNT(DISTINCT fo.order_id) AS first_orders_count,
  ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS first_order_revenue,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(oi.sale_price), COUNT(DISTINCT fo.order_id)), 2) AS first_order_aov
FROM first_orders_in_window AS fo
LEFT JOIN order_items AS oi
  ON fo.order_id = oi.order_id
 AND oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1 ASC;
report: Over the trailing 12 months (2025-10-01 to 2026-09-01), new customer acquisition—defined by each customer's earliest order timestamp—and initial spend—computed from initial order line items excluding Cancelled and Returned items—demonstrated substantial volume growth alongside stable order values. Monthly new customer acquisition nearly doubled from 1664 customers in 2025-10-01 (with a period low of 1635 in 2025-11-01) to a high of 3136 customers in 2026-09-01. In line with customer volume, first_order_revenue expanded from 100935.04 in 2025-10-01 to 202971.55 in 2026-09-01. Meanwhile, initial average order value remained relatively steady throughout the year, ranging between 60.66 in 2025-10-01 and 68.09 in 2026-05-01, ending at 64.72 in 2026-09-01. A key follow-up worth checking is whether recent cohorts—particularly 2026-09-01—have pending returns that have not yet been processed, which could lower net initial revenue once return windows close.

question: What share of our revenue and orders came from new versus returning customers last quarter?
approach: Classifies customers as 'New' if their earliest order in the orders table occurred during the previous calendar quarter, and 'Returning' if their first order was prior to that quarter. Revenue is summed from order_items (excluding Cancelled and Returned items) and order volume from distinct order_ids within the last quarter window. The query outputs total revenue, order count, AOV, and revenue contribution percentage across both customer segments.
sql:
WITH customer_first_order AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    MIN(created_at) AS first_order_at
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY user_id
),
quarter_bounds AS (
  SELECT
    TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER), QUARTER)) AS start_ts,
    TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER)) AS end_ts
)
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN cfo.first_order_at >= qb.start_ts THEN 'New'
    ELSE 'Returning'
  END AS customer_type,
  COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS total_orders,
  ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS total_revenue,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(oi.sale_price), COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)), 2) AS aov,
  ROUND(
    100.0 * SAFE_DIVIDE(
      SUM(oi.sale_price),
      SUM(SUM(oi.sale_price)) OVER ()
    ),
    2
  ) AS revenue_share_pct
FROM order_items AS oi
CROSS JOIN quarter_bounds AS qb
JOIN customer_first_order AS cfo
  ON oi.user_id = cfo.user_id
WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
  AND oi.created_at >= qb.start_ts
  AND oi.created_at < qb.end_ts
GROUP BY 1;
report: Customers were defined as "New" if their earliest recorded order occurred during the previous calendar quarter and "Returning" if their first order predated that quarter, with revenue derived from order items excluding cancelled and returned items. Last quarter, New customers accounted for 7648 total orders and 658695.27 in total revenue, representing a 61.88% revenue share with an AOV of 86.13. Returning customers drove 4799 total orders and 405698.23 in total revenue, contributing 38.12% of revenue with an AOV of 84.54. As a follow-up, it is worth verifying how far back the historical orders table extends to ensure that older customer purchases were not truncated and misclassifying returning buyers as new.

question: Which high-value customers have churned in the last 90 days, and what was their lifetime spend?
approach: Identifies churned customers as those who placed at least one order historically but have had zero orders within the last 90 days. Aggregates lifetime spend from order_items, excluding Cancelled and Returned statuses, and counts distinct lifetime orders. The list is sorted by total historical spend descending to surface the most valuable lost accounts.
sql:
WITH customer_orders AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS lifetime_orders,
    MAX(created_at) AS last_order_at
  FROM orders
  GROUP BY user_id
  HAVING MAX(created_at) < TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)
),
customer_spend AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    ROUND(SUM(sale_price), 2) AS lifetime_spend
  FROM order_items
  WHERE status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT
  co.user_id,
  u.country,
  co.lifetime_orders,
  DATE(co.last_order_at) AS last_order_date,
  COALESCE(cs.lifetime_spend, 0.0) AS lifetime_spend,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(cs.lifetime_spend, co.lifetime_orders), 2) AS lifetime_aov
FROM customer_orders AS co
JOIN users AS u
  ON co.user_id = u.id
LEFT JOIN customer_spend AS cs
  ON co.user_id = cs.user_id
ORDER BY lifetime_spend DESC
LIMIT 50;

question: Who are our top 50 customers by spend so far this year, and what is their order frequency and average order value?
approach: Calculates customer spend and order count for non-cancelled and non-returned line items created since the start of the current calendar year (DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR)). Joins order_items with users to aggregate spend and distinct orders per customer, computing average order value (AOV) via SAFE_DIVIDE. Results are ranked by total spend descending and limited to the top 50 customers while keeping personal data masked.
sql:
SELECT

  COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS total_orders,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(oi.sale_price), COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)), 2) AS aov

question: Which active customers in the US are underspending relative to their state's median AOV over the last 90 days?
approach: Filters for active customers in the United States who placed at least one order in the last 90 days. Computes each customer's AOV across non-cancelled, non-returned items, and calculates the state median AOV using PERCENTILE_CONT partitioned by state and country. Flags underspending customers whose AOV falls below their state's median and ranks them by the largest deficit below the median.
sql:
WITH active_users AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)
),
user_aov_90d AS (
  SELECT
    u.id AS user_id,
    u.state,
    u.country,
    COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders_count,
    ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS total_spend,
    ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(oi.sale_price), COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)), 2) AS customer_aov
  FROM users AS u
  JOIN active_users AS au
    ON u.id = au.user_id
  JOIN order_items AS oi
    ON u.id = oi.user_id
  WHERE u.country = 'United States'
    AND oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)
  GROUP BY u.id, u.state, u.country
  HAVING orders_count > 0
),
state_medians AS (
  SELECT
    user_id,
    state,
    country,
    orders_count,
    total_spend,
    customer_aov,
    ROUND(PERCENTILE_CONT(customer_aov, 0.5) OVER(PARTITION BY state, country), 2) AS state_median_aov
  FROM user_aov_90d
)
SELECT
  user_id,
  state,
  country,
  orders_count,
  total_spend,
  customer_aov,
  state_median_aov,
  ROUND(state_median_aov - customer_aov, 2) AS aov_deficit
FROM state_medians
WHERE customer_aov < state_median_aov
ORDER BY aov_deficit DESC
LIMIT 50;
report: This analysis evaluates active US customers who placed at least one order in the last 90 days, measuring each customer's AOV across non-cancelled, non-returned items against their state's median AOV computed via `PERCENTILE_CONT`. The customer with the largest gap is `897a47f5eac7128f` in New Hampshire, whose `customer_aov` of 14.67 falls 76.32 below the `state_median_aov` of 90.99 across 1 order. Following closely are `865641041af4a9ac` in Rhode Island with an `aov_deficit` of 68.51 (`customer_aov` of 16.99 vs. `state_median_aov` of 85.5) and `1121f2f7fbe5686c` in Alaska with an `aov_deficit` of 68.12 (`customer_aov` of 28.88 vs. `state_median_aov` of 97.0). A key caveat worth checking is that 19 of the top 20 underspending customers have an `orders_count` of only 1 (with customer `b4c5b6186bd4c949` having 2), meaning these deficits reflect isolated low-value purchases rather than established spending trends; verifying order history across a longer timeframe would help determine if these customers represent genuine engagement opportunities.

question: Can I see our revenue, order count, and AOV broken down by customer age group for last quarter?
approach: Group customers into demographic age brackets from users.age and join with order_items on user_id. Filter order item creation dates to the previous full calendar quarter using DATE_TRUNC and DATE_SUB against CURRENT_DATE(). Exclude items with status 'Cancelled' or 'Returned' to compute net revenue and order count, then calculate AOV using SAFE_DIVIDE.
sql:
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN u.age < 18 THEN '<18'
    WHEN u.age BETWEEN 18 AND 24 THEN '18-24'
    WHEN u.age BETWEEN 25 AND 34 THEN '25-34'
    WHEN u.age BETWEEN 35 AND 44 THEN '35-44'

  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(oi.sale_price), COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id)), 2) AS aov
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN users AS u
  ON oi.user_id = u.id
WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
  AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER), QUARTER))
  AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))

question: Which demographic segments by age band and gender have the highest customer lifetime value and purchase frequency?
approach: Calculate each customer's lifetime net spend and order count from order_items, excluding Cancelled and Returned line items, and join with users to obtain demographic attributes (age band and gender). Group by demographic segment to compute average customer lifetime value (LTV) and average orders placed per customer. Sort results by average customer LTV descending to highlight top-performing segments.
sql:
WITH customer_aggregates AS (
  SELECT
    u.id AS user_id,
    u.gender,
    CASE
      WHEN u.age < 25 THEN '<25'
      WHEN u.age BETWEEN 25 AND 34 THEN '25-34'
      WHEN u.age BETWEEN 35 AND 44 THEN '35-44'
      WHEN u.age BETWEEN 45 AND 54 THEN '45-54'
      WHEN u.age >= 55 THEN '55+'
      ELSE 'Unknown'
    END AS age_band,
    COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS total_orders,
    SUM(oi.sale_price) AS lifetime_spend
  FROM users AS u
  JOIN order_items AS oi
    ON u.id = oi.user_id
  WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
  GROUP BY u.id, u.gender, age_band
)
SELECT
  age_band,
  gender,
  COUNT(user_id) AS total_customers,
  ROUND(AVG(total_orders), 2) AS avg_orders_per_customer,
  ROUND(AVG(lifetime_spend), 2) AS avg_customer_ltv,
  ROUND(SUM(lifetime_spend), 2) AS total_segment_revenue
FROM customer_aggregates
GROUP BY age_band, gender
ORDER BY avg_customer_ltv DESC
LIMIT 50

In terms of purchase frequency, females aged 55+ have the highest rate at 1.43 orders per customer (with an average LTV of 116.67), closely followed by males aged 55+, males under 25, and females aged 25-34 at 1.42 orders per customer. Across all age brackets, male segments exhibit higher average LTVs (124.69 to 130.02) than female segments (112.4 to 116.67), despite order frequency remaining relatively flat between 1.40 and 1.43 across all groups. As a follow-up, it is worth checking customer account tenure or acquisition dates across these segments, as differing customer lifespans could influence cumulative lifetime spend and order counts.

question: How do our traffic sources compare on revenue and AOV when broken down by gender over the last 90 days?
approach: Join order_items with users on user_id to classify transactions by traffic source and gender. Filter to the trailing 90 days from CURRENT_TIMESTAMP() and exclude Cancelled and Returned items per the glossary revenue definition. Aggregate total net sales, distinct orders, and calculate AOV using SAFE_DIVIDE.
sql:
SELECT
  u.traffic_source,
  u.gender,
  COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS total_orders,
  COUNT(DISTINCT oi.user_id) AS customer_count,
  ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS total_revenue,

question: Over the last 12 months, what share of our revenue came from repeat buyers versus first-time buyers across age groups?
approach: Rank orders sequentially per customer using ROW_NUMBER() over orders partitioned by user_id to identify first orders versus repeat orders. Join order_items created within the last 365 days to this order sequence and to users to categorize by age band. Exclude Cancelled and Returned items, summing revenue separately for first-time and repeat orders to compute the repeat revenue contribution percentage.
sql:
WITH order_sequence AS (
  SELECT
    order_id,
    user_id,
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at) AS order_num
  FROM orders
  WHERE status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
)
SELECT
  CASE
    WHEN u.age < 25 THEN '<25'
    WHEN u.age BETWEEN 25 AND 34 THEN '25-34'
    WHEN u.age BETWEEN 35 AND 44 THEN '35-44'
    WHEN u.age BETWEEN 45 AND 54 THEN '45-54'
    WHEN u.age >= 55 THEN '55+'
    ELSE 'Unknown'
  END AS age_band,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN os.order_num = 1 THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS first_order_revenue,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN os.order_num > 1 THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS repeat_order_revenue,
  ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS total_revenue,
  ROUND(
    SAFE_DIVIDE(
      SUM(CASE WHEN os.order_num > 1 THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END),
      SUM(oi.sale_price)
    ) * 100,
    2
  ) AS repeat_revenue_pct
FROM order_items AS oi
JOIN order_sequence AS os
  ON oi.order_id = os.order_id
JOIN users AS u
  ON oi.user_id = u.id
WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
  AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 365 DAY)
GROUP BY age_band
ORDER BY age_band
report: Over the last 365 days, repeat orders were identified by ranking each customer's lifetime order sequence, with revenue calculated from non-cancelled and non-returned order items. Repeat buyers generated between 36.22% and 38.96% of total revenue across all age bands, with the highest share observed in the 55+ group at 38.96% (repeat revenue of 340521.12 vs. first-order revenue of 533573.54; total 874094.66) and the 25-34 group at 38.85% (repeat revenue of 212034.33 vs. first-order revenue of 333724.99; total 545759.32). The remaining segments were the <25 group at 37.39% (repeat revenue of 271279.35 vs. first-order revenue of 454257.93; total 725537.28), the 45-54 group at 36.64% (repeat revenue of 204594.58 vs. first-order revenue of 353729.05; total 558323.63), and the 35-44 group at 36.22% (repeat revenue of 199069.93 vs. first-order revenue of 350572.09; total 549642.02). As a follow-up, it is worth checking customer acquisition dates to determine whether variations in repeat revenue share are influenced by the tenure and size of older customer cohorts compared to newly acquired users.

question: Which traffic sources have the highest customer churn rates, and how many active customers does each channel have today?
approach: Apply the glossary definitions for customer activity: active customers placed at least one order in the last 90 days, while churned customers placed an order prior to the last 90 days but none within the last 90 days. Filter orders to valid statuses (excluding Cancelled and Returned) and join with users on user_id to group by traffic_source. Compute churn rate as churned customers divided by customers active before the 90-day window.
sql:
WITH customer_activity AS (
  SELECT
    u.traffic_source,
    o.user_id,
    MAX(CASE WHEN o.created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS ordered_last_90d,
    MAX(CASE WHEN o.created_at < TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS ordered_prior
  FROM orders AS o
  JOIN users AS u
    ON o.user_id = u.id
  WHERE o.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
  GROUP BY u.traffic_source, o.user_id
)
SELECT
  traffic_source,
  COUNTIF(ordered_last_90d = 1) AS active_customers,
  COUNTIF(ordered_prior = 1 AND ordered_last_90d = 0) AS churned_customers,
  COUNTIF(ordered_prior = 1) AS customers_prior,
  ROUND(
    SAFE_DIVIDE(
      COUNTIF(ordered_prior = 1 AND ordered_last_90d = 0),
      COUNTIF(ordered_prior = 1)
    ) * 100,
    2
  ) AS churn_rate_pct
FROM customer_activity
GROUP BY traffic_source
ORDER BY churn_rate_pct DESC
report: Based on the analysis, active customers are defined as those with at least one non-cancelled, non-returned order in the last 90 days, while churned customers ordered prior to this window but not within it (with churn rate calculated against customers active prior to the 90-day cutoff). Organic traffic shows the highest churn rate at 93.91% with 1849 active customers, closely followed by Search at 93.6% (8832 active customers), Display at 93.57% (530 active customers), Email at 93.52% (659 active customers), and Facebook at 93.3% (843 active customers). While churn rates remain remarkably uniform across channels (ranging from 93.3% to 93.91%), Search maintains by far the largest active customer volume. A recommended follow-up is to verify whether the 90-day window aligns with the typical repurchase cycle of the product catalog, as category reorder cadences may heavily influence these churn figures.

question: What is the repeat purchase rate and average order frequency across our customer acquisition traffic sources?
approach: Aggregate completed and valid orders per customer from orders, excluding Cancelled and Returned records, and join to users to identify each customer's acquisition traffic_source. Calculate repeat buyers as customers with 2 or more distinct lifetime orders. Compute repeat purchase rate as repeat buyers over total purchasing customers per acquisition channel using SAFE_DIVIDE.
sql:
WITH customer_orders AS (
  SELECT
    u.traffic_source,
    u.id AS user_id,
    COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders
  FROM users AS u
  JOIN orders AS o
    ON u.id = o.user_id
  WHERE o.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
  GROUP BY u.traffic_source, u.id
)
SELECT
  traffic_source,
  COUNT(user_id) AS total_purchasers,
  COUNTIF(total_orders >= 2) AS repeat_purchasers,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNTIF(total_orders >= 2), COUNT(user_id)) * 100, 2) AS repeat_purchase_rate_pct,
  ROUND(AVG(total_orders), 2) AS avg_orders_per_customer
FROM customer_orders
GROUP BY traffic_source
ORDER BY repeat_purchase_rate_pct DESC
report: Based on completed and valid orders (excluding Cancelled and Returned records), repeat buyers were defined as customers with two or more distinct lifetime orders, with the repeat purchase rate calculated as repeat buyers divided by total purchasing customers per acquisition channel. Across all sources, metrics remain remarkably consistent: Organic recorded a 30.72% repeat purchase rate and 1.42 average orders per customer (3,042 repeat out of 9,903 total purchasers), followed by Search at 30.59% and 1.41 average orders (14,140 repeat out of 46,223 total purchasers), and Facebook at 30.59% and 1.42 average orders (1,246 repeat out of 4,073 total purchasers). Display achieved a 30.41% repeat purchase rate with 1.41 average orders per customer (821 repeat out of 2,700 total purchasers), while Email had a 29.72% repeat purchase rate with 1.4 average orders per customer (998 repeat out of 3,358 total purchasers). As a follow-up, it is worth evaluating customer tenure and cohort maturation by acquisition channel, as lifetime purchase counts may be constrained if newer customers have not had adequate time to place a second order.

question: How many open orders have been stuck in processing for more than 48 hours, and what is the merchandise value at risk?
approach: Identify open orders stuck in processing by filtering orders where status is 'Processing', shipped_at is NULL, and created_at is more than 48 hours before CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(). Join to order_items on order_id to aggregate merchandise value at risk (sale_price), excluding cancelled or returned items. Average the pending elapsed days using TIMESTAMP_DIFF.
sql:
SELECT
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS stuck_orders_count,
  COUNT(oi.id) AS total_items,
  ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS total_value_at_risk,
  ROUND(AVG(TIMESTAMP_DIFF(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), o.created_at, HOUR) / 24.0), 2) AS avg_days_pending
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi
  ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
WHERE o.status = 'Processing'
  AND o.shipped_at IS NULL
  AND o.created_at <= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 48 HOUR)
  AND oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned');
report: There are 24,513 open orders (encompassing 35,606 items) that have been stuck in processing for more than 48 hours, representing a total merchandise value at risk of 2,115,989.19. Per the analysis approach, stuck orders were defined as having a status of 'Processing', a null 'shipped_at' timestamp, and a 'created_at' timestamp older than 48 hours, with merchandise value calculated from item sale prices excluding returned or cancelled items. Across these affected orders, the average elapsed time pending is 705.06 days. A critical follow-up is to investigate whether legacy test records or upstream fulfillment integration failures are artificially inflating this queue, given that an average pending duration of 705.06 days suggests many orders have been abandoned rather than freshly delayed.

question: Which product categories had the longest average shipping turnaround times last month?
approach: Evaluate dispatch turnaround from item placement (created_at) to shipment (shipped_at) at the line item level across product categories. Join order_items to products on product_id for items created in the previous calendar month. Exclude cancelled or returned items, filter for items with non-null shipping timestamps, and rank categories by longest average dispatch time.
sql:
SELECT
  p.category,
  COUNT(DISTINCT oi.id) AS shipped_units,
  COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS distinct_orders,
  ROUND(AVG(TIMESTAMP_DIFF(oi.shipped_at, oi.created_at, HOUR) / 24.0), 2) AS avg_dispatch_days,
  ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS total_shipped_revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN products p
  ON oi.product_id = p.id
WHERE oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 MONTH), MONTH))
  AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH))
  AND oi.shipped_at IS NOT NULL
  AND oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY avg_dispatch_days DESC
LIMIT 50;
report: Shipping turnaround times were measured at the line item level as the duration from item creation (`created_at`) to dispatch (`shipped_at`) for items created in the previous calendar month, excluding cancelled or returned records and unfulfilled items without shipment timestamps. Based on this definition, **Clothing Sets** had the longest average turnaround time at 1.81 `avg_dispatch_days` (7 shipped units, 7 distinct orders, and 607.82 total shipped revenue), followed by **Socks & Hosiery** at 0.79 days (105 shipped units), **Socks** at 0.76 days (171 shipped units), **Suits** at 0.7 days (34 shipped units), and **Outerwear & Coats** at 0.66 days (226 shipped units). As a follow-up, it is worth checking whether the leading category's average was skewed by specific outliers, given that Clothing Sets had a notably small volume of only 7 shipped units compared to the other top categories.

question: What percentage of our shipped orders took more than 3 days to ship each month this year?
approach: Identify delayed shipments defined as orders taking more than 72 hours (3 days) between created_at and shipped_at. Filter orders created in the current year that have shipped, grouping by month of order creation. Compute the percentage of shipped orders that experienced delays using SAFE_DIVIDE.
sql:
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), MONTH) AS order_month,
  COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS total_shipped_orders,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
    WHEN TIMESTAMP_DIFF(shipped_at, created_at, HOUR) > 72 THEN order_id
  END) AS delayed_orders,
  ROUND(
    SAFE_DIVIDE(
      COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN TIMESTAMP_DIFF(shipped_at, created_at, HOUR) > 72 THEN order_id END) * 100.0,
      COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)
    ),
    2
  ) AS delayed_shipment_rate_pct
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR))
  AND shipped_at IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY order_month ASC;
report: Based on the provided data, delayed shipments are defined as shipped orders created in the current year where the elapsed time between `created_at` and `shipped_at` exceeds 72 hours (3 days). Across all 10 reported months from `2026-01-01` through `2026-10-01`, the `delayed_shipment_rate_pct` was `0.0`, with `0` `delayed_orders` recorded in each month. Monthly volume varied from a low of `1893` `total_shipped_orders` in `2026-02-01` to a high of `4144` in `2026-09-01`. As a follow-up, it is worth verifying the data pipeline and the accuracy of the `shipped_at` timestamps, as zero delays across thousands of monthly shipments may indicate a logging anomaly or default timestamp population.

question: How have our average fulfillment and transit times trended by month over the last 90 days?
approach: Calculate processing duration (created_at to shipped_at) and transit duration (shipped_at to delivered_at) in days from the orders table. Filter for completed orders placed in the last 90 days that have recorded delivery timestamps. Group by the month of order creation and average the durations using SAFE_DIVIDE or AVG.
sql:
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), MONTH) AS order_month,
  COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS delivered_orders,
  ROUND(AVG(TIMESTAMP_DIFF(shipped_at, created_at, HOUR) / 24.0), 2) AS avg_processing_days,
  ROUND(AVG(TIMESTAMP_DIFF(delivered_at, shipped_at, HOUR) / 24.0), 2) AS avg_transit_days,
  ROUND(AVG(TIMESTAMP_DIFF(delivered_at, created_at, HOUR) / 24.0), 2) AS avg_total_delivery_days
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY)
  AND delivered_at IS NOT NULL
  AND shipped_at IS NOT NULL
  AND status = 'Complete'
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY order_month ASC;
report: Over the analyzed period, fulfillment (processing) duration was defined as order creation to shipment (`created_at` to `shipped_at`), and transit duration was defined as shipment to delivery (`shipped_at` to `delivered_at`) for completed orders grouped by creation month. Average processing times remained virtually flat, tracking at 1.51 days in 2026-07-01 (819 delivered orders), 1.48 days in 2026-08-01 (1307 orders), 1.48 days in 2026-09-01 (1628 orders), and 1.49 days in 2026-10-01 (1209 orders). Average transit times also remained steady after an initial decrease from 2.57 days in 2026-07-01 to 2.45 days in 2026-08-01, followed by 2.49 days in 2026-09-01 and 2.48 days in 2026-10-01 (yielding average total delivery days of 4.1, 3.94, 4.0, and 3.99, respectively). As a follow-up caveat, filtering strictly for orders with recorded delivery timestamps may bias the most recent month (2026-10-01) toward artificially shorter transit times, as slower shipments placed late in the month may still be in transit.

question: What was our order status mix last quarter in terms of order volume and percentage of total orders?
approach: Count distinct orders grouped by status for orders created during the previous calendar quarter. Compute each status's share of total quarterly orders using SAFE_DIVIDE against the overall volume. Note that order status reflects the latest lifecycle state of orders placed within that time window.
sql:
WITH quarterly_orders AS (
  SELECT
    status,
    COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS order_count
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER), QUARTER))
    AND created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))
  GROUP BY status
),
total_orders AS (
  SELECT SUM(order_count) AS total_count FROM quarterly_orders
)
SELECT
  qo.status,
  qo.order_count,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(qo.order_count * 100.0, t.total_count), 2) AS pct_of_total_orders
FROM quarterly_orders qo
CROSS JOIN total_orders t
ORDER BY qo.order_count DESC;

These figures represent distinct orders created during the previous calendar quarter, with percentage shares calculated against total quarterly volume. Each order's status reflects its latest lifecycle state as of the time the data was pulled. question: Which countries have had the slowest average delivery times over the last 180 days, and how many orders did they receive?
approach: Measure total elapsed time from order placement (created_at) to arrival (delivered_at) in days for orders placed in the last 180 days. Join orders to users on user_id to associate destination country, filtering for completed orders with populated delivery timestamps. Filter out low-volume countries with a minimum volume threshold of 20 orders to minimize sample bias.
sql:
SELECT
  u.country,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS completed_orders,
  ROUND(AVG(TIMESTAMP_DIFF(o.delivered_at, o.created_at, HOUR) / 24.0), 2) AS avg_delivery_days,
  ROUND(AVG(TIMESTAMP_DIFF(o.shipped_at, o.created_at, HOUR) / 24.0), 2) AS avg_processing_days,
  ROUND(AVG(TIMESTAMP_DIFF(o.delivered_at, o.shipped_at, HOUR) / 24.0), 2) AS avg_transit_days
FROM orders o
JOIN users u
  ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 180 DAY)
  AND o.status = 'Complete'
  AND o.shipped_at IS NOT NULL
  AND o.delivered_at IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY u.country
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) >= 20
ORDER BY avg_delivery_days DESC
LIMIT 50;

Among qualifying destinations, the slowest average delivery times were recorded by Spain at 4.13 average delivery days (312 completed orders), South Korea at 4.09 days (392 orders), and the United Kingdom at 4.07 days (331 orders). question: Which countries have the highest churn rate among customers who were active before the last 90 days?
approach: A churned customer is defined as someone who placed at least one order before the last 90 days and none during the last 90 days. We aggregate orders by user to flag prior and recent purchase history, join to users to capture country, and calculate the churn rate as churned divided by historically active customers. We filter out countries with small customer samples to avoid noisy percentages.
sql:
WITH customer_history AS (
  SELECT
    u.id AS user_id,
    u.country,
    MAX(CASE WHEN o.created_at < TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS active_prior,
    MAX(CASE WHEN o.created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 90 DAY) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS active_recent
  FROM users u
  JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
  GROUP BY u.id, u.country
)
SELECT
  country,
  COUNTIF(active_prior = 1) AS prior_active_customers,
  COUNTIF(active_prior = 1 AND active_recent = 0) AS churned_customers,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(
    COUNTIF(active_prior = 1 AND active_recent = 0),
    COUNTIF(active_prior = 1)
  ), 4) AS churn_rate
FROM customer_history
WHERE active_prior = 1
GROUP BY country
HAVING prior_active_customers >= 50
ORDER BY churn_rate DESC
LIMIT 50
report: Based on the provided data, Belgium exhibits the highest churn rate at 0.929 (772 churned customers out of 831 prior active customers), followed by Germany at 0.9284 (2786 churned out of 3001) and the United Kingdom at 0.9217 (2967 churned out of 3219). Under this approach, a churned customer is defined as an individual who placed at least one order before the last 90 days and zero orders during the last 90 days, with the churn rate calculated as churned customers divided by prior active customers. Churn rates across all 12 reported countries are closely clustered between 0.9107 (Australia) and 0.929 (Belgium). As a follow-up, it is worth reviewing the specific minimum sample size threshold applied, as country volumes vary considerably from 149 prior active customers in Poland to 23597 in China.

question: What is our item return rate and net revenue by country over the last 12 months?
approach: Item return rate is calculated as the count of returned items divided by total items ordered. Net revenue includes all items except those with status 'Cancelled' or 'Returned'. We join order_items to users on user_id over the trailing 12 months (365 days) and aggregate by normalized country name.
sql:
SELECT
  u.country,
  COUNT(oi.id) AS total_items,
  COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned') AS returned_items,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned'), COUNT(oi.id)), 4) AS return_rate,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS net_revenue
FROM order_items oi
JOIN users u ON oi.user_id = u.id
WHERE oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP_SUB(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(), INTERVAL 365 DAY)
GROUP BY u.country
ORDER BY net_revenue DESC
LIMIT 50

Across the 14 recorded countries, China generated the highest net revenue at 1096787.67 with 24379 total items, 2421 returned items, and a return rate of 0.0993, followed by the United States (net revenue of 731292.68; return rate of 0.1067 on 16142 items) and Brazil (net revenue of 490095.82; return rate of 0.0961 on 10861 items). Return rates among major markets remained near 10%, while smaller-volume countries showed more variance, ranging from 0.0 in Austria (1 total item, net revenue of 25.0) to 0.1437 in Poland (160 total items, net revenue of 7414.36) and 0.2 in Colombia (10 total items, net revenue of 603.77). question: Can you break down revenue, order volume, and customer count by country and state for this year to show our top regional markets globally?
approach: Because region and state names can recur across different countries, we group by both users.country and users.state. Revenue sums order_items.sale_price excluding 'Cancelled' and 'Returned' rows, dated by order_items.created_at within the current calendar year. Total orders and distinct purchasers are also counted per region.
sql:

question: How did net revenue grow quarter-over-quarter across our top state markets between last quarter and the quarter before?
approach: Net revenue excludes cancelled and returned line items and is aggregated by country and state for two quarters: the previous quarter (Q-1) and the quarter prior (Q-2). Always pairing state with country prevents collisions across international jurisdictions. Percentage growth is calculated using SAFE_DIVIDE comparing the two periods.
sql:
WITH quarterly_sales AS (
  SELECT
    u.country,
    u.state,
    SUM(CASE
      WHEN oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 2 QUARTER), QUARTER))
       AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER), QUARTER))
       AND oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
      THEN oi.sale_price
      ELSE 0
    END) AS revenue_prior_quarter,
    SUM(CASE
      WHEN oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER), QUARTER))
       AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))
       AND oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
      THEN oi.sale_price
      ELSE 0
    END) AS revenue_last_quarter
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN users u ON oi.user_id = u.id
  WHERE oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 2 QUARTER), QUARTER))
    AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))
  GROUP BY u.country, u.state
)
SELECT
  country,
  state,
  ROUND(revenue_prior_quarter, 2) AS revenue_prior_quarter,
  ROUND(revenue_last_quarter, 2) AS revenue_last_quarter,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(revenue_last_quarter - revenue_prior_quarter, revenue_prior_quarter) * 100, 2) AS revenue_growth_pct
FROM quarterly_sales
WHERE revenue_prior_quarter > 0
ORDER BY revenue_last_quarter DESC
LIMIT 50
report: Net revenue—defined as revenue excluding cancelled and returned line items and paired by country and state—grew across all top state markets between the prior quarter (Q-2) and last quarter (Q-1). The highest-earning market was Guangdong, China, which grew 52.62% quarter-over-quarter from 38291.42 to 58440.25, followed by England, United Kingdom, which rose 43.12% from 29793.0 to 42641.08, and California, United States, which grew 29.78% from 29345.16 to 38084.53. Growth rates varied considerably across other leading regions, ranging from 96.7% in Hebei, China (12231.83 to 24059.61) and 75.18% in São Paulo, Brazil (15145.2 to 26532.07) to a more modest 6.25% in Zhejiang, China (17928.63 to 19049.74). A key follow-up worth checking is retrieving the remaining 30 rows of the 50 total markets in the result set to assess whether these strong growth trends hold across smaller state jurisdictions.

question: What are our top 10 countries by net revenue and active customer count over the last 90 days?
approach: Net revenue is calculated as the sum of order_items.sale_price excluding items with status 'Cancelled' or 'Returned'. question: Which US states generated the highest revenue last quarter, and what was the average order value in each?
approach: Revenue is the sum of order_items.sale_price excluding cancelled and returned items, dated by order_items.created_at, and AOV divides revenue by distinct orders. We filter users to the United States and restrict line items to the previous completed calendar quarter using DATE_TRUNC. State and country are both selected to maintain geographical precision.
sql:
SELECT
  u.country,
  u.state,
  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS net_revenue,
  COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.order_id END) AS orders,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(
    SUM(CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END),
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') THEN oi.order_id END)
  ), 2) AS aov
FROM order_items oi
JOIN users u ON oi.user_id = u.id
WHERE u.country = 'United States'
  AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER), QUARTER))

Per the defined methodology, revenue reflects the sum of `order_items.sale_price` excluding cancelled and returned items dated by line item `created_at` for the previous completed quarter, and average order value (AOV) is calculated by dividing net revenue by distinct orders. question: Which brands are driving the highest gross profit this year, and what are their margin percentages?
approach: Gross margin is defined as sale_price minus products.cost on order_items excluding status 'Cancelled' and 'Returned', dated by order_items.created_at. question: Which of our top 10 brands saw the biggest drop in gross margin rate comparing last quarter to the quarter before it?

Gross margin is sale_price minus cost excluding 'Cancelled' and 'Returned' orders. We calculate the percentage point difference between the two quarters to identify brands suffering margin compression.
sql:
WITH brand_performance AS (
  SELECT
    p.brand,
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE(oi.created_at), QUARTER) AS quarter_date,
    SUM(oi.sale_price) AS revenue,
    SUM(oi.sale_price - p.cost) AS margin
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p
    ON oi.product_id = p.id
  WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 2 QUARTER), QUARTER))
    AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))
    AND p.brand IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY p.brand, quarter_date
),
top_brands AS (
  SELECT brand
  FROM brand_performance
  GROUP BY brand
  ORDER BY SUM(revenue) DESC
  LIMIT 10
),
quarterly_rates AS (
  SELECT
    bp.brand,
    MAX(CASE WHEN bp.quarter_date = DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 2 QUARTER), QUARTER)
        THEN SAFE_DIVIDE(bp.margin, bp.revenue) * 100 END) AS prev_q_margin_pct,
    MAX(CASE WHEN bp.quarter_date = DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER), QUARTER)
        THEN SAFE_DIVIDE(bp.margin, bp.revenue) * 100 END) AS last_q_margin_pct
  FROM brand_performance bp
  JOIN top_brands tb
    ON bp.brand = tb.brand
  GROUP BY bp.brand
)
SELECT
  brand,
  ROUND(prev_q_margin_pct, 2) AS two_quarters_ago_margin_pct,
  ROUND(last_q_margin_pct, 2) AS last_quarter_margin_pct,
  ROUND(last_q_margin_pct - prev_q_margin_pct, 2) AS margin_pct_change
FROM quarterly_rates
ORDER BY margin_pct_change ASC
LIMIT 50

question: Which product categories grew the fastest in revenue last quarter compared to the prior quarter?
approach: Joins order_items and products across the last two completed calendar quarters, excluding Cancelled and Returned items. Segregates revenue by quarter using conditional aggregation and computes dollar growth alongside percentage growth via SAFE_DIVIDE. Filters out categories with zero prior quarter revenue to avoid division by zero anomalies and ranks by highest growth rate.
sql:
WITH quarter_boundaries AS (
  SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER), QUARTER) AS last_quarter_start,
    DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER) AS last_quarter_end,
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 2 QUARTER), QUARTER) AS prior_quarter_start
),
category_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    p.category,
    SUM(CASE
      WHEN DATE(oi.created_at) >= qb.last_quarter_start AND DATE(oi.created_at) < qb.last_quarter_end
      THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END) AS last_quarter_revenue,
    SUM(CASE
      WHEN DATE(oi.created_at) >= qb.prior_quarter_start AND DATE(oi.created_at) < qb.last_quarter_start
      THEN oi.sale_price ELSE 0 END) AS prior_quarter_revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
  CROSS JOIN quarter_boundaries qb
  WHERE oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(qb.prior_quarter_start)
    AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(qb.last_quarter_end)
    AND oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
  GROUP BY p.category
)
SELECT
  category,
  ROUND(prior_quarter_revenue, 2) AS prior_quarter_revenue,
  ROUND(last_quarter_revenue, 2) AS last_quarter_revenue,
  ROUND(last_quarter_revenue - prior_quarter_revenue, 2) AS revenue_change,
  ROUND(100.0 * SAFE_DIVIDE(last_quarter_revenue - prior_quarter_revenue, prior_quarter_revenue), 2) AS revenue_growth_pct
FROM category_revenue
WHERE prior_quarter_revenue > 0
ORDER BY revenue_growth_pct DESC
LIMIT 50

question: Which brands had the biggest increase in cancellation rates comparing last quarter to the quarter before that?
approach: Aggregate order_items by brand for the last quarter and the prior quarter using DATE_TRUNC with QUARTER. Calculate the cancellation rate for each quarter as cancelled items over total items, then compute the percentage point difference between the two periods. Filter for brands with sufficient volume in both quarters to prevent small-sample noise.
sql:
WITH brand_quarters AS (
  SELECT
    p.brand,
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE(oi.created_at), QUARTER) AS order_quarter,
    COUNT(*) AS total_items,
    COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Cancelled') AS cancelled_items,
    SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Cancelled'), COUNT(*)) AS cancellation_rate
  FROM order_items AS oi
  JOIN products AS p
    ON oi.product_id = p.id
  WHERE oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER), INTERVAL 2 QUARTER))
    AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))
  GROUP BY p.brand, order_quarter
),
quarter_pivots AS (
  SELECT
    brand,
    MAX(CASE WHEN order_quarter = DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER), INTERVAL 2 QUARTER) THEN total_items END) AS prior_qtr_items,
    MAX(CASE WHEN order_quarter = DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER), INTERVAL 2 QUARTER) THEN cancellation_rate END) AS prior_qtr_cancel_rate,
    MAX(CASE WHEN order_quarter = DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER) THEN total_items END) AS last_qtr_items,
    MAX(CASE WHEN order_quarter = DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER), INTERVAL 1 QUARTER) THEN cancellation_rate END) AS last_qtr_cancel_rate
  FROM brand_quarters
  GROUP BY brand
)
SELECT
  brand,
  prior_qtr_items,
  ROUND(prior_qtr_cancel_rate * 100, 2) AS prior_qtr_cancel_rate_pct,
  last_qtr_items,
  ROUND(last_qtr_cancel_rate * 100, 2) AS last_qtr_cancel_rate_pct,
  ROUND((last_qtr_cancel_rate - prior_qtr_cancel_rate) * 100, 2) AS cancel_rate_diff_pct_points
FROM quarter_pivots
WHERE prior_qtr_items >= 50
  AND last_qtr_items >= 50
  AND last_qtr_cancel_rate IS NOT NULL
  AND prior_qtr_cancel_rate IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY cancel_rate_diff_pct_points DESC
LIMIT 50

Tommy Bahama saw the second-largest jump, increasing 9.62 percentage points from 14.52% (62 items) to 24.14% (58 items), followed by Anna-Kaci with a 9.28 percentage point rise from 8.0% (50 items) to 17.28% (81 items). question: What is our monthly gross revenue, net revenue, and return rate over the past 12 months?
approach: Analyze order_items over the last 12 full calendar months by aggregating gross revenue (excluding cancelled items), net revenue (excluding cancelled and returned items), and total line items. Calculate the monthly return rate as the count of returned items divided by all ordered items according to the glossary definition.

SELECT

  ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN status != 'Cancelled' THEN sale_price ELSE 0 END), 2) AS gross_revenue,

  COUNT(id) AS total_items,

question: Show me our monthly revenue, order volume, and units sold over the last 12 full months.
approach: Aggregate order_items for net revenue (sale_price excluding Cancelled and Returned) and sold units, and aggregate orders for distinct order counts, attributing each by their respective created_at timestamps per the business glossary. Filter both sets to the last 12 completed calendar months using CURRENT_DATE(). Join the aggregated months to compute Average Order Value (AOV) using SAFE_DIVIDE.
sql:
WITH item_metrics AS (
  SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), MONTH) AS order_month,
    ROUND(SUM(sale_price), 2) AS revenue,
    COUNT(id) AS units_sold
  FROM order_items
  WHERE status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH), INTERVAL 12 MONTH))
    AND created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH))
  GROUP BY 1
),
order_metrics AS (
  SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), MONTH) AS order_month,
    COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS total_orders
  FROM orders
  WHERE status NOT IN ('Cancelled')
    AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH), INTERVAL 12 MONTH))
    AND created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH))
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  i.order_month,
  i.revenue,
  o.total_orders,
  i.units_sold,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(i.revenue, o.total_orders), 2) AS aov
FROM item_metrics i
JOIN order_metrics o ON i.order_month = o.order_month
ORDER BY i.order_month DESC
LIMIT 50;

question: How has monthly revenue split between Men's and Women's departments over the last 6 months?
approach: Join order_items to products on product_id to categorize revenue by department (Men vs Women). Filter out Cancelled and Returned items over the last 6 full calendar months. Compute total revenue by month and department, then use a window function across the month to determine each department's percentage share of that month's net revenue.
sql:
WITH monthly_dept_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE(oi.created_at), MONTH) AS revenue_month,
    p.department,
    ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
  WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH), INTERVAL 6 MONTH))
    AND oi.created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH))
  GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT
  revenue_month,
  department,
  revenue,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(revenue, SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY revenue_month)) * 100, 2) AS revenue_share_pct
FROM monthly_dept_revenue
ORDER BY revenue_month DESC, department ASC
LIMIT 50;

question: How have our average order value and basket size trended quarterly over the last 2 years?
approach: Summarize net revenue and total units sold from order_items and distinct order counts from orders by calendar quarter over the last 8 quarters (2 years), applying proper created_at attribution to each table. Filter out Cancelled and Returned statuses for valid sales volume, then calculate Average Order Value (revenue / orders) and average units per order (units / orders) using SAFE_DIVIDE.
sql:
WITH quarterly_items AS (
  SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), QUARTER) AS quarter,
    ROUND(SUM(sale_price), 2) AS revenue,
    COUNT(id) AS units
  FROM order_items
  WHERE status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER), INTERVAL 8 QUARTER))
    AND created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))
  GROUP BY 1
),
quarterly_orders AS (
  SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), QUARTER) AS quarter,
    COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders
  FROM orders
  WHERE status NOT IN ('Cancelled')
    AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER), INTERVAL 8 QUARTER))
    AND created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  i.quarter,
  i.revenue,
  o.orders,
  i.units,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(i.revenue, o.orders), 2) AS aov,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(i.units, o.orders), 2) AS units_per_order
FROM quarterly_items i
JOIN quarterly_orders o ON i.quarter = o.quarter
ORDER BY i.quarter DESC
LIMIT 50;

question: What is our quarterly revenue and quarter-over-quarter revenue growth rate for the past 8 quarters?
approach: Aggregate order_items by calendar quarter over the prior 8 completed quarters using DATE_TRUNC with QUARTER. Net revenue excludes items with status Cancelled or Returned. Use the LAG analytic window function to fetch the preceding quarter's revenue and compute Quarter-over-Quarter (QoQ) percentage growth with SAFE_DIVIDE.
sql:
WITH quarterly_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), QUARTER) AS quarter,
    ROUND(SUM(sale_price), 2) AS revenue
  FROM order_items
  WHERE status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER), INTERVAL 8 QUARTER))
    AND created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), QUARTER))
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT
  quarter,
  revenue,
  LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY quarter) AS prev_quarter_revenue,
  ROUND(
    SAFE_DIVIDE(revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY quarter), LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY quarter)) * 100,
    2
  ) AS qoq_growth_pct
FROM quarterly_revenue
ORDER BY quarter DESC
LIMIT 50;

question: Compare our monthly revenue year-over-year for each month so far this year versus the same months last year.
approach: Group order_items by calendar month number for the current year-to-date and the equivalent year-to-date period of the prior year. Filter out Cancelled and Returned items. Self-join the two periods on month number to calculate year-over-year revenue difference and YoY growth percentage using SAFE_DIVIDE.
sql:
WITH monthly_revenue AS (
  SELECT
    EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at) AS order_year,
    EXTRACT(MONTH FROM created_at) AS order_month_num,
    FORMAT_TIMESTAMP('%B', created_at) AS month_name,
    ROUND(SUM(sale_price), 2) AS revenue
  FROM order_items
  WHERE status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned')
    AND (
      (created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR)) AND created_at < CURRENT_TIMESTAMP())
      OR (
        created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR), INTERVAL 1 YEAR))
        AND created_at < TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 YEAR))
      )
    )
  GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
)
SELECT
  curr.order_month_num,
  curr.month_name,
  curr.revenue AS current_year_revenue,
  prev.revenue AS previous_year_revenue,
  ROUND(curr.revenue - prev.revenue, 2) AS yoy_growth_amount,
  ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(curr.revenue - prev.revenue, prev.revenue) * 100, 2) AS yoy_growth_pct
FROM monthly_revenue curr
LEFT JOIN monthly_revenue prev
  ON curr.order_month_num = prev.order_month_num
  AND prev.order_year = curr.order_year - 1
WHERE curr.order_year = EXTRACT(YEAR FROM CURRENT_DATE())
ORDER BY curr.order_month_num ASC
LIMIT 50;

Monthly year-over-year growth percentages ranged from 37.97% in February (current year revenue of 182891.15 versus 132562.46 last year) to 148.53% in September, which saw current year revenue reach a high of 417952.72 compared to 168171.26 previously. October recorded the highest overall increase by volume with a yoy_growth_amount of 257105.22 (current year revenue of 295918.98 versus 38813.76), resulting in a 662.41% growth rate. A key follow-up is to verify whether October represents partial-month data for either year or if an anomaly explains the steep drop in previous year revenue to 38813.76.
